title: Stochastic learning approach for binary optimization: Application to Bayesian optimal design of experiments
contribution: Recasts binary Bayesian OED (sensor placement) as minimising the expected utility over a product-Bernoulli distribution and solves it by a policy-gradient (REINFORCE-type) stochastic method with an optimal baseline, avoiding relaxation, rounding, design gradients and smoothing of the l0 penalty.
problem_entry: The relax-then-round route to binary OED needs design gradients (many model solves), smoothing of l0, and gives relaxed solutions not guaranteed to be related to binary ones (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Minimise Upsilon(theta) = E_{zeta~Bernoulli(theta)} J(zeta) over theta in [0,1]^ns with a score-function gradient estimate that needs only J values at sampled designs; add an optimal baseline for variance reduction (pp. 5, 10, 14-17).
assumptions: Independent Bernoulli activations; linear forward operators and A-optimality in the experiments; convergence in expectation only under a Robbins-Monro step schedule (pp. 3, 5, 9, 13, 28).
proof_devices: Convex-hull lifting: [0,1]^ns = conv{0,1}^ns, values of Upsilon = conv of objective values, agreement at vertices, hence equal minima (Proposition 3.1, Caratheodory, pp. 6-7)
Uniqueness transfer: a unique binary optimum is the unique theta-optimum (Lemma 3.2, p. 7)
Unbiased bounded-variance estimator meets an assumption of a cited SGD convergence theorem (Lemma 3.4 used on p. 13)
experiments: 2-D linear toy (p. 18) and 14-candidate advection-diffusion sensor placement with all 16,384 designs enumerated as ground truth; with the optimal baseline the sampled designs fall within 1% of the global optimum in 20 iterations (pp. 22-24).
positioning: Contrasts with relaxation plus l1/continuation/sum-up-rounding and with earlier Robbins-Monro/SAA stochastic OED; links the method to policy-gradient reinforcement learning (pp. 2-3, 10).
writing: Contributions paragraph enumerated First/Second/Third/Fourth against the standard approach (pp. 2-3); the benefits of the reformulation are listed again in five points after the proofs (pp. 7-8).
limits_future: Learning-rate choice is the main open issue; comparison with sample average approximation deferred to separate work (p. 28); the saving over relaxation is argued from model-solve counts (pp. 16-18), not from a run in the parts read.

method_links.note: Re-casts the binary design problem into stochastic optimisation / RL policy gradient, not into Leyffer's NLP or filter base
Honest ground truth by full enumeration, but the headline saving over relaxation is argued from cost formulas, not measured on the same problem
Reformulation chosen so the nonsmooth l0 penalty can be used without smoothing (weak)

transferable: Benchmark binary-design methods at an enumerable size (2^14) and report the distance to the true global optimum under a small fixed iteration budget (pp. 22-24).
Justify a lifted formulation by three facts: convex hull of the domain, convex hull of the values, agreement at the vertices; equal optimal values follow (pp. 6-7).

quotes.text: In general, however, the numerical solutions of the two problems are not guaranteed to be related or even similar.
We also note that Algorithm 3.1 is equivalent to the vanilla policy gradient REINFORCE algorithm [51].

title: Sequential linearization method for bound-constrained mathematical programs with complementarity constraints
contribution: Proposes SLPCC, a trust-region method that solves a separable LPCC each iteration while keeping complementarity feasible, proves convergence to B-stationary points, and adds Cauchy and bound-constrained-QP steps for speed, as a subproblem solver for an augmented Lagrangian method for MPCCs.
problem_entry: Bound-constrained MPCCs arise as augmented Lagrangian subproblems of general MPCCs after slack variables are added; no analysed trust-region method keeps complementarity feasible in every iterate (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Linearise f, keep complementarity, use an l-infinity trust region so the LPCC separates into 1-D LPs and 2-D LPCCs solved by checking at most four points; accept by actual over linear-predicted reduction, reset the radius to at least a fixed value (Algorithm 1, Props 2.3-2.4, pp. 3-6).
assumptions: f C^1 with locally Lipschitz gradient (Assumption 4.1, p. 8); feasible start obtained by projection (p. 4); no coercivity, unboundedness detected numerically (p. 9); C^2 for the second-order steps (p. 14).
proof_devices: Constructive B-stationarity test: a feasible descent direction for some partition of the biactive set (Proposition 4.1, p. 8)
Three-lemma skeleton: Taylor reduction bound, finite inner loop, step with reduction bounded below by a multiple of the radius near a non-B-stationary point (Lemmas 4.3-4.5, outline p. 9)
Radius reset to at least a fixed value keeps the radius from collapsing (p. 7)
Acceleration steps accepted only if as good as the first-order step, changing only a factor 1/2 in the proof (p. 16)
experiments: Python; 40 random QPs (indefinite/PSD, n0=n1=20,40) and 20 nonlinear instances vs filterSQP, IPOPT, MINOS, SNOPT on the x1'x2<=0 reformulation; iteration violin plots and a performance profile with failures counted (pp. 17-20).
positioning: Places itself beside Scholtes-Stohr trust-region penalty, Fukushima-Tseng epsilon-active sets and active-set methods of Judice et al. and Chen-Goldfarb (p. 2); states that NLP solvers are currently the most efficient MPEC solvers (p. 17).
writing: A two-variable example motivating the design comes before the proofs (pp. 6-7); the proof is announced with an outline paragraph (p. 9); limits are stated plainly in the results (pp. 17-20).
limits_future: Plain method at best linear (p. 17); slower in time than filterSQP, MINOS, SNOPT, cauchy often slowest, attributed to Python (pp. 19-20); degenerate instances counted as failures (p. 19); extension to AMPL-style mixed complementarity without slacks (pp. 21-22).

method_links.note: Two-variable MPCC on which exact-Hessian SQP converges to an M-stationary, non-B-stationary point; stated as the reason to use linear models
NLP trust-region toolkit and the SLQP idea carried into MPCCs, with a bound-constrained QP on the identified active set
Failures counted, filtered MINOS runs named, per-iteration cost differences stated, time losses reported
NLP baselines get the inequality complementarity form x1'x2<=0, with a citation that the equality form is worse

When comparing with SQP or interior-point codes, say that iteration counts only check for a reasonable number of outer iterations and report each solver's own times (p. 17).
Detect unboundedness by a large-negative objective test in the code instead of assuming coercivity (p. 9).

title: A mixed-integer PDE-constrained optimization formulation for electromagnetic cloaking
contribution: Formulates binary electromagnetic cloak design (2-D Helmholtz, nominal and uncertain incidence angle) as a MIPDECO and solves it by relaxation, rounding and a first-order trust-region method whose subproblem is a knapsack over a Hamming ball.
problem_entry: Cloak design is usually done by topology optimisation; here it is posed as a MIPDECO with one binary per design cell, then extended to an expected objective over uncertain incidence angles (pp. 3-5).
key_idea: Solve the relaxation with reduced-space quasi-Newton (TAO blmvm), round at tau=0.8, then improve with a steepest-descent trust-region method: linearised objective, l1 (Hamming) trust region giving a knapsack, nonlinear trust-region acceptance rule; one forward and one adjoint solve per iteration (pp. 11-13).
assumptions: Discretised 2-D Helmholtz with absorbing boundary (FEniCS 128x128 mesh, k0=6pi, q=0.75); bilinear state equation makes the relaxation nonconvex; method explicitly heuristic, stopping at Delta<1 (pp. 11-14).
proof_devices: No convergence theorem in the parts read; nonconvexity shown numerically by evaluating J along the segment between two checkerboard designs (pp. 14-15)
l1 trust region on binaries rewritten as an affine knapsack constraint (eq. 4.4, p. 12)
experiments: Three cloak regions x two angles, 20x20 and 40x40 control meshes; 25 random starts; 15-79 TR iterations; PDE/gradient time dominates and knapsack solves are cheap; 10- and 15-angle uncertainty runs; no external MINLP or topology-optimisation baseline (pp. 13-20).
positioning: Alternative to topology-optimisation cloaking (Haslinger-Makinen); read as rounding plus repeated local branching (Fischetti-Lodi; Nannicini-Belotti-Liberti) but first-order; builds on the Hahn-Sager-Leyffer discrete trust-region report (pp. 3, 12).
writing: Short applied paper: formulation, adjoints, algorithm, numerical evidence; the conclusion restates the method and gives no future work (pp. 21-22).
limits_future: Relaxation is not a valid lower bound and rounding can beat it (pp. 15, 18); direct MINLP with discretised PDEs ruled out from experience on other MIPDECOs (p. 12); no future directions stated (pp. 21-22).

method_links.note: Nonlinear trust-region acceptance rule carried unchanged into a binary PDE design problem
Formulation chosen around solver capability: full-space MINLP with discretised PDEs avoided because modern MINLP solvers cannot solve it; rounding-threshold choice reported with its effect
No external baselines; evidence is random starts, relaxation and rounding only

title: BROOD: Bilevel and robust optimization and outlier detection for efficient tuning of high-energy physics event generators
contribution: Automates the choice of observable weights in Monte Carlo event-generator tuning through bilevel (surrogate-based outer search) and single-level robust formulations, with outlier-observable and chi-square bin filtering, compared with the ATLAS A14 expert tune on three new metrics.
problem_entry: Expert hand-weighting of observables in generator tuning is slow, subjective, 'inefficient and biased' (pp. 4, 7).
key_idea: Bilevel: weights on the simplex chosen by a merit function (portfolio or median/mean score) with an RBF surrogate over the black-box inner fit; robust: worst-case bin deviation with slacks and a mu-controlled weight lower bound; pre-filter outlier observables by Z-score and bins by a longest-contiguous-run chi-square test solved by a maximum-subarray algorithm (pp. 9-16).
assumptions: Bins independent (pp. 7, 50); rational surrogate represents the MC simulation; discrepancies come from the model's domain, not analysis mistakes (p. 13); multimodal inner problem handled by 100 multistarts (p. 17).
proof_devices: n/a (no theorems); chi-square degrees of freedom reduced to |B|-d because bins share parameters (p. 15)
Contiguous bin selection posed as an integer program and solved in polynomial time via maximum subarray (eq. 15, p. 16)
experiments: ATLAS A14 and Sherpa datasets; bilevel (three merits), robust, Expert and all-weights-equal compared on weighted chi-square, A-optimality and log D-optimality; no method best on all metrics, Expert best on two of three for the full data; about 14.5 h for bilevel vs weeks or months by hand (pp. 17-18, 23, 38-40).
positioning: Related to influence-based weighting [5] and Bayesian-optimisation tuning without weights [6]; builds on the Professor framework, now apprentice (pp. 6-7).
writing: Physics-facing exposition with a notation table (pp. 7-8); the conclusion lists four contributions as First-Fourth (p. 50).
limits_future: Sherpa optimal parameters often on the box bounds, suggesting missing physics or a too-small domain; a trust-region outer loop is proposed as future work; bin correlations ignored (p. 50).

method_links.note: Human expert tune kept as a named baseline; split verdict by metric reported rather than a winner (Leyffer's share unknown)
Bilevel problem replaced by a single-level robust formulation with slacks because it is easier to solve (weak for Leyffer personally)

transferable: When automation replaces expert judgement, keep the expert's result as a named baseline, score both on several objective metrics, and report where the expert still wins (pp. 17, 23).
Before calling a MIP solver on a subset-selection problem with a contiguity constraint, check whether it reduces to a maximum-subarray scan (p. 16).
Filter data the model cannot describe: fit each observable alone, flag outliers among the ideal per-observable errors, give them weight zero (p. 14).
coauthors: Wenjing Wang, Mohan Krishnamoorthy, Juliane Müller, Stephen Mrenna, Holger Schulz, Xiangyang Ju, Zachary Marshall

title: Improving Earth System Predictability with Artificial Intelligence
contribution: A two-page SIAM News report of the DOE AI4ESP workshop that summarises AI/ML for Earth system models and lists applied-math challenges, including constrained learning and the inclusion of state-of-the-art optimisation methods.
problem_entry: Impressions from the October 2021 AI4ESP workshop (450+ attendees, 150+ white papers), ahead of the official report (p. 3).
key_idea: n/a (no method); summarises talks by Schneider, Gentine, Shen and Zanna (pp. 3-4) and closes with the authors' list of applied-math challenges (p. 4).
positioning: Reports others' talks in their voice; cites differentiable convex optimisation layers and physics-informed ML (p. 4).
writing: News-style summary organised by speaker, ending with an applied-math challenge paragraph (pp. 3-4).
limits_future: Open challenges: learning emerging constraints, identifying erroneous constraints, including state-of-the-art optimisation methods, explainable AI, rare-event identification (p. 4).
